claim: Only two E3 ligases are routinely used for PROTAC development.
source: Proteolysis-targeting chimeras (PROTACs) enable the selective and sub-stoichiometric elimination of pathological proteins, yet only two E3 ligases are routinely used for this purpose.
evidence: Stated in the abstract as a motivation for the study

claim: Most degrader molecules developed to date have exploited only two E3 ligases, VHL (von Hippel-Lindau) and CRBN (Cereblon).
source: Despite the widespread clinical and academic use of PROTACs, most degrader molecules developed to date have exploited only two E3 ligases, VHL (von Hippel-Lindau) and CRBN (Cereblon) (Buckley et al., 2012; Winter et al., 2015).
evidence: Supported by citations to Buckley et al., 2012 and Winter et al., 2015

claim: Several additional E3 ligases have been reported in the literature as being PROTAC-compatible.
source: While several additional E3 ligases have been reported in the literature as being PROTAC-compatible, these ligands do not have well-understood mechanisms of E3 engagement and often do not fully degrade their target substrates (Ishida and Ciulli, 2021).
evidence: Supported by citation to Ishida and Ciulli, 2021

claim: Additional E3 ligases reported as PROTAC-compatible do not have well-understood mechanisms of E3 engagement and often do not fully degrade their target substrates.
source: While several additional E3 ligases have been reported in the literature as being PROTAC-compatible, these ligands do not have well-understood mechanisms of E3 engagement and often do not fully degrade their target substrates (Ishida and Ciulli, 2021).
evidence: Supported by citation to Ishida and Ciulli, 2021

claim: KLHDC2 (Kelch-like homology domain-containing protein 2) has emerged as a promising candidate for PROTAC development.
source: Among potential E3 ligases for PROTAC development, KLHDC2 (Kelch-like homology domain-containing protein 2) has emerged as a promising candidate (Békés et al., 2022).
evidence: Supported by citation to Békés et al., 2022

claim: KLHDC2 is a CUL2 adaptor protein.
source: A CUL2 adaptor protein, KLHDC2, serves as a key component of the C-end degron pathway, recognizing C-terminal diglycine residues of client proteins, promoting their ubiquitination and degradation (Pilcher et al., 2025).
evidence: Supported by citation to Pilcher et al., 2025

claim: KLHDC2 serves as a key component of the C-end degron pathway.
source: A CUL2 adaptor protein, KLHDC2, serves as a key component of the C-end degron pathway, recognizing C-terminal diglycine residues of client proteins, promoting their ubiquitination and degradation (Pilcher et al., 2025).
evidence: Supported by citation to Pilcher et al., 2025

claim: KLHDC2 recognizes C-terminal diglycine residues of client proteins, promoting their ubiquitination and degradation.
source: A CUL2 adaptor protein, KLHDC2, serves as a key component of the C-end degron pathway, recognizing C-terminal diglycine residues of client proteins, promoting their ubiquitination and degradation (Pilcher et al., 2025).
evidence: Supported by citation to Pilcher et al., 2025

claim: Client proteins of KLHDC2 include selenocysteine-containing proteins, like SelK (Selenoprotein K).
source: Client proteins of KLHDC2 include selenocysteine-containing proteins, like SelK (Selenoprotein K), which, in the context of selenocysteine depletion, undergo premature translational termination, revealing a C-terminal diglycine degron (Rusnac et al., 2018).
evidence: Supported by citation to Rusnac et al., 2018

claim: In the context of selenocysteine depletion, selenocysteine-containing proteins undergo premature translational termination, revealing a C-terminal diglycine degron.
source: Client proteins of KLHDC2 include selenocysteine-containing proteins, like SelK (Selenoprotein K), which, in the context of selenocysteine depletion, undergo premature translational termination, revealing a C-terminal diglycine degron (Rusnac et al., 2018).
evidence: Supported by citation to Rusnac et al., 2018

claim: Recognition of the diglycine degron of SelK by KLHDC2 in its Kelch beta propellor domain is characterized by low nanomolar dissociation constants (<10 nM).
source: Previous work has shown that recognition of the diglycine degron of SelK by KLHDC2 in its Kelch beta propellor domain is characterized by low nanomolar dissociation constants (<10 nM) and with favorable binding kinetics for PROTAC development (Figure 1A; Rusnac et al., 2018).
evidence: Supported by citation to Rusnac et al., 2018

claim: Recognition of the diglycine degron of SelK by KLHDC2 has favorable binding kinetics for PROTAC development.
source: Previous work has shown that recognition of the diglycine degron of SelK by KLHDC2 in its Kelch beta propellor domain is characterized by low nanomolar dissociation constants (<10 nM) and with favorable binding kinetics for PROTAC development (Figure 1A; Rusnac et al., 2018).
evidence: Supported by citation to Rusnac et al., 2018

claim: Unbiased protein proximity-based screens for generalizable E3 degraders have indicated that KLHDC2 is among the best E3 ligases for fully degrading generic protein substrates.

claim: From approximately 14,000 primary screening hits, 51 displayed dose-responsive inhibitory signals in follow-up assays.

claim: KEAP1 (Kelch-like ECH-associated protein 1) has been co-opted for targeted protein degradation using PROTACs.
